title: Knowledge check: Professional Project Organization

questions.prompt: For “Professional Project Organization”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Professional Project Organization is one step in Debugging, Testing, and Software Quality; errors, warnings, assertions and tests provide distinct signals. Reproducible failing cases help isolate defects. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Professional Project Organization” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Organizing Source Code and Data” as part of lesson 208. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Professional Project Organization” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Test expected behavior and edge cases, avoid leaking sensitive values in logs, and run checks in a clean environment. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
